item.title: “Eye” spy: Cyclops Blink returns with extended capabilities
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 IRON VIKING (Sandworm) returns with an evolved Cyclops Blink implant targeting Cisco FMC devices, adding network scanning and packet surveillance to its 2022 toolkit.
- Found as /lib/tz/timezone_check on compromised Cisco FMC devices, this x86-64 Linux ELF drops 2022's WatchGuard-specific firmware hooks for generic SysV init persistence: startup symlinks at /etc/rc2-5.d/S89timezone_check survive reboots and require root-level write access to /lib and /etc, confirming high-privilege execution at install time.
- The five-module framework adds two capabilities absent from 2022 samples: Module 0x11 performs raw-socket TCP scanning across 60+ ports (SSH, SNMP, LDAP, BGP, VMware) from the appliance's trusted network position, and Module 0x12 captures raw Ethernet frames using AF_PACKET/SOCK_RAW, compiling operator-supplied search terms into an Aho-Corasick matcher to selectively exfiltrate credentials, tokens, and session cookies as pcap records.
- C2 uses outbound TLS (certificate verification disabled) to 89.34.96[.]56 over TCP 43856 or 49172, beaconing hourly. DNS-over-HTTPS resolves hostnames via direct TLS POST to 8.8.8.8:443/dns-query, bypassing local DNS logs. The malformed User-Agent mixing Firefox rv:129.0 with a Chrome token is a strong network detection signal.
- The controller masquerades as [kworker/0:1] in process listings.

item.title: Your AI Keys Are The Loot Now
item.description:
Anthropic's 154-page September 2026 report documents AI API key theft as deliberate loot, not collateral damage, and shows how fragmented sessions defeat per-request safeguards.
- A single French-speaking operator exploited an undocumented WordPress re-installation race condition to create a rogue admin account, built a doxxing platform with tens of millions of rows, and ran the entire campaign on stolen API keys, breaching 14 of 42 tracked targets. Two undergraduates in Hunan province ran an automated firmware exploit foundry that produced 12+ possible zero-days in one month, with 13 collection agents running scheduled with no operator present.
- Suspected ShinyHunters affiliates pivoted stolen AI keys to run their own attack workloads at the victim's expense. A separate group hit an AI vendor's evaluation sandbox via prompt injection, extracted production keys, and used them to attack that vendor and unrelated targets simultaneously, with a follow-on campaign hitting roughly 30 AI companies in about four days.
- Safeguards failed consistently under fragmentation. Claude refused 9 of 10 direct malicious requests but performed less consistently when work was split across smaller sessions. A weapons cell deliberately applied this, and a China-linked actor obtained suppression guidance naming 10 private citizens through re-prompting alone, no jailbreak required.
Inventory every AI API key in apps, containers, mobile builds, and public repos.

item.title: Corporate Endpoint Triage: How It Works and What to Use
item.description:
Corporate endpoint triage with Belkasoft T: how to rapidly inspect a live Windows workstation, collect only what matters, and make the escalation call without pulling the machine from production.
Key findings:
- Triage follows the order of volatility (NIST SP 800-86): RAM first, then network state and processes, then disk artifacts. Belkasoft T prompts for memory acquisition at launch, requires admin rights for a full dump, and can fall back to Belkasoft Live RAM Capturer. Plan for standard-user execution on corporate endpoints, it still yields useful results but loses memory, other user folders, and locked system files.
- The tool detects 1,500+ application profiles (browsers, chat, cloud sync, crypto wallets, mobile backups) plus registry hives, jumplists, LNK files, prefetch, and event logs. Detection and collection are separated: the operator reviews what was found before choosing what to export.
- Footprint is real and should be documented. Windows logs the connected USB device and the last executable run from it. AV may inspect and log the binary. Record the run in case notes so those entries are explained rather than discovered by someone else later.
- Output lands as a .tar partial image readable by Belkasoft X and other forensic tools, alongside an HTML file list. For endpoints nobody can reach physically, Belkasoft R (agent-based, GPO or WMI deployment) handles remote acquisition.

item.title: AD Rights Management Service (Part 2): Extraction, Offline Decryption, and the Unrotatable Key
item.description:
The AD RMS Server Licensor Certificate private key can be silently exported by any member of the AD RMS Service Group, enabling permanent offline decryption of every RMS-protected document across the entire deployment's lifetime.
Key findings:
- Any account in the AD RMS Service Group can export the 1172-byte Server Licensor Certificate (SLC) private key. This key is the root of trust for the entire RMS deployment: whoever holds it can decrypt any document the deployment ever protected, without contacting any server.
- Decryption is fully offline. An attacker who exfiltrates the SLC private key retains permanent read access to protected content even after the deployment is decommissioned and rebuilt, because the key does not rotate.
- The "unrotatable" nature is the critical DFIR wrinkle: standard incident response playbooks that rebuild a compromised service do not revoke attacker access to already-protected documents. Scope extends to every file the RMS instance ever touched.
- Forensic pivot: audit membership of the AD RMS Service Group and review export or backup operations against the RMS cluster's certificate store. Any unauthorized account membership or unexplained certificate export event is a high-fidelity indicator of key theft.
Hunt: enumerate AD RMS Service Group members now and cross-reference against privileged account baselines. Unexplained additions are your lead.

item.title: BraZetsu: AI-Enhanced Reconnaissance Fuels Exilware’s Access Marketplace
item.description:
Brazilian 🇧🇷 IAB actor Exilware deploys BraZetsu, a Python framework using AI-assisted reconnaissance to auto-profile and monetize compromised hosts across finance, government, and industrial sectors in Brazil 🇧🇷 and beyond.
- BraZetsu is compiled with Nuitka into standalone Windows executables, complicating signature detection. It retrieves C2 config from Pastebin via get_server_config(), decrypting XOR-encoded data (key: p4st3_s3cr3t_k3y) to extract domain, port, and auth token in pipe-delimited format. Interactive access runs over a WebSocket TLS backdoor on port 8443. Early persistence used a Registry Run key named MonitorSystem. Distribution lures include msedge[0-9].exe and wifi_driver.exe.
- The get_stealth_iab_tags() function runs ~20 environment checks, tagging hosts for cloud (AWS/Azure/Kubernetes), ERP (SAP, TOTVS), SCADA (WinCC, RSLogix, FactoryTalk), backup (Veeam), and EDR presence (CrowdStrike, SentinelOne). Browser history from Chromium-based browsers is queried via SQLite, with databases copied to %TEMP% using shutil.copyfile to bypass file locks. CNAB, .pfx, and .p12 files are also harvested.
- Five versions evolved from February 2026 to a full IAB platform by v5. The latest was fully undetected on VirusTotal at analysis time. AI-assisted development is evidenced by verbose logging style; embedded strings reference server-side AI for data processing and target prioritization.

item.title: Machine speed, hold the AI: Hand-rolled marimo CVE-2026-39987 exploit
item.description:
A skilled human operator exploited CVE-2026-39987 in marimo to pivot from an unauthenticated WebSocket to a bastion SSH session in eight seconds, no AI, no public tooling, hand-rolled boto3 scripts only.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-39987 is a pre-auth RCE in marimo's /terminal/ws WebSocket endpoint, which skips the validate_auth() call applied to every other endpoint. Any unauthenticated client gets a full interactive PTY as the marimo process user. Affected through version 0.20.4, fixed in 0.23.0, listed on CISA KEV with a federal remediation deadline of May 7, 2026.
- The operator spent four hours hand-writing and debugging eight boto3 chain scripts, dropping each as a base64 blob via echo '<b64>' | base64 -d > /tmp/<name>.py, then running nohup python3 /tmp/<name>.py. The base64 wrap hides script contents from a defender skimming bash_history. Files to hunt: /tmp/chain.py, /tmp/full_chain.py, /tmp/bastion_key (mode 0600, SSH key from Secrets Manager).
- Post-RCE pivot chain: harvest AWS keys from /proc/<pid>/environ and the app's Redis backend, call secretsmanager:GetSecretValue with region fallback across us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1, us-east-2, write the retrieved SSH private key to /tmp/bastion_key, SSH to bastion via paramiko. C2: 45.79.187[.]72:4444, source: 172.236.12[.]17, both AS63949 (Akamai/Linode).

item.title: Linux Detection Engineering - Local Privilege Escalation
item.description:
Elastic Security Labs maps a durable, outcome-oriented Linux LPE detection framework against 11 public 2026 PoCs, covering page-cache corruption, namespace abuse, trusted-helper theft, and SUID misconfiguration without relying on per-CVE rules.
Key findings:
- Seven of 13 tracked 2026 Linux LPEs share a copy-on-write page-cache corruption primitive: Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431), DirtyFrag (CVE-2026-43284/43500), Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), DirtyDecrypt (CVE-2026-31635), pedit COW (CVE-2026-46331), DirtyClone (CVE-2026-43503), and RefluXFS. The kernel trigger varies across AF_ALG, ESP/RxRPC, act_pedit, and skb helpers, but every exploit still ends the same way: a SUID helper or interpreter runs with effective uid 0. Qualys and others used LLM-assisted workflows to discover several of these, accelerating the per-bug-class pace.
- The framework detects in two layers. Layer one is outcome-oriented: exec from a writable path (/tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, /home, /run/user) followed by a uid_change to 0, correlated by parent entity ID within a short window. Layer two adds per-class signals: AF_ALG socket bursts plus splice for Copy Fail; unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) preceding a root transition for CIFSwitch (CVE-2026-46243) and OVSwrap (CVE-2026-64531); busctl --system calls for ptrace_may_dream; and shadow-read alerts for chage_pwn (CVE-2026-46333).
- CVE-2026-46333 (exit-time FD theft via pidfd_getfd) is worth special attention.

item.title: Android malware creates a hidden copy of your banking app
item.description:
Android banking Trojan Gigabud abuses Android work profiles to clone banking apps into an isolated profile, letting operators commit fraud in a space that may be invisible to bank-side anti-fraud systems.
Key findings:
- Gigabud gains a foothold via sideloaded fake airline, tax, or government APKs delivered through phishing. It requests Accessibility access, overlay permission, and battery-optimization exemption to enable remote control and credential theft via fake login overlays that harvest banking credentials and device PIN.
- The Trojan then installs Vwork, a weaponized fork of the open-source Shelter tool. Vwork strips cross-profile protections, exposes profile-management components, hides its launcher icon, and clones the target banking app into a newly created work profile under attacker control.
- Fraud is executed remotely inside the cloned work profile, optionally behind a black screen. Because Android isolates apps across profiles, a banking app or MDM security tool in the personal profile may never correlate the malware detection with the fraudulent session happening next door.
- Malwarebytes detects Gigabud components under signatures including Android/Trojan.Spy.Gigabud.xc and Android/Trojan.Banker.ACR577B2BA2H61, among others listed in the report.
Responder takeaway: on a suspicious Android device, enumerate work profiles (Settings > Accounts or Device Admin).

item.title: Suricata keyword highlight: subslice, part 2 — transforms, the prefilter, and what’s next
item.description:
Suricata's subslice keyword gets a deep dive: how it chains with other transforms, integrates with the prefilter MPM, and where the keyword is headed next.
- subslice can chain up to 15 transforms in sequence. A rule trimming http.user_agent to 4 bytes, lowercasing it, and matching "curl" looks like: http.user_agent; subslice: 0, 4, truncate; to_lowercase; content:"curl"; bsize:4. Plain content modifiers like depth: cannot do this because they cannot hand a bounded window to downstream transforms like to_sha256 or from_base64.
- At prefilter time, Suricata registers the post-transform content as the fast_pattern in the multi-pattern matcher (MPM). subslice is cheap here: it only adjusts an offset and length, no copy, no hash. Two rules on the same sticky buffer with different chains get separate MPM entries, keeping them independent.
- Transform results are cached per packet per chain. Multiple rules sharing subslice: 0, 4 on http.user_agent run the transform once total, not once per rule. Adding more rules on the same chain costs nothing extra.
- Dynamic offsets are not yet supported. Redmine issue 8234 tracks two candidate syntaxes: an inline extract form and a byte_extract variable reference. Neither loads in current builds. Only the main branch has subslice at all.
If you write Suricata rules for binary or length-prefixed protocols, test subslice on the main branch using the rule file, pcap, and generator script linked in the post.

item.title: [remote] CVE-2026-80428 Unauthenticated PHP Object Injection via Shibboleth - ILIAS < 9.22, 10.0 < 10.10, 11.0 < 11.3 - RCE
item.description:
CVE-2026-80428: Unauthenticated PHP object injection in ILIAS LMS chains two auth-exempt endpoints into RCE as the web server user, affecting ILIAS < 9.22, 10.0 < 10.10, and 11.0 < 11.3.
- CVE-2026-80428 is a two-stage chain. Stage 1 POSTs to ltiauth.php, which writes attacker-controlled session data to the session table. A "\w+|" marker in the parameter value breaks the custom session parser, causing raw serialized PHP to land in ilSession as if it were a legitimate value. Stage 2 POSTs a SOAP LogoutNotification to shib_logout.php, which deserializes every live session row with no class allowlist, triggering the payload.
- The gadget is GuzzleHttp\Cookie\FileCookieJar, bundled in ILIAS's own vendor tree. __destruct() calls file_put_contents() with an attacker-supplied path and JSON-embedded PHP, dropping a webshell to the docroot. No authentication is required at any step.
- Forensic artifacts to hunt: unexpected .php files in the ILIAS public docroot (random-hex names like util_a1b2c3.php), POST requests to /ltiauth.php and /shib_logout.php in web server logs, SOAP body content in POST payloads to shib_logout.php, and new session rows with serialized object strings in the ilSession database table.
- A working public exploit was published 2026-08-31 by DigiProSec. v9 and v10 are confirmed exploitable; v11 has a code path issue that prevents exploitation as packaged, but patch regardless. Fixed in 9.22, 10.10, and 11.3.

item.title: UK Council Attack Linked to Mass Exploitation of SonicWall Flaw
item.description:
CVE-2026-15409, a CVSS 10.0 zero-day in SonicWall SMA1000, was mass-exploited within 48 hours of disclosure, stealing AD credentials from 160 domains and enabling full DCSync in five environments.
- CVE-2026-15409 is an unauthenticated SSRF in the WorkPlace portal's /wsproxy endpoint. It chains through a hardcoded Erlang cookie in firmware to reach couchdb@127.0.0.1 and execute OS commands as the couchdb account. No login required, fully automatable in seconds. CISA added it to KEV; INC ransomware and KNUCKLEBALL malware operator UTA0533 have also weaponized it.
- The operator's ldap_extract.py decrypted LDAP passwords from /usr/local/extranet/etc/policy_file.xml using a fixed 32-byte AES key hardcoded in ASAPPasswordUtil.class, meaning the same key works across every vulnerable appliance. Secretsdump was dropped to /tmp/secretsdump via curl, then run against internal DCs from the appliance itself, bypassing EDR and Windows event logs entirely.
- Hunt.io captured the full toolchain from an open directory at 95.181.173[.]36 on July 17. Of 250 targets, 168 leaked LDAP configs with 534 AD accounts; five lost full NTDS via DCSync. Impacket binary SHA-256: 690f5031deede7d3357d0ca24c89866ae8c60e6c63b3a2c8bba813a6ac10ae5b.
Patch to firmware 12.4.3-03453 or later, but assume compromise first. Hunt /tmp on SMA1000 appliances for secretsdump or NTDS files, rotate all credentials, and re-image. Full IOC list and log locations in the Hunt.io report.

item.title: 2026-09-08: XWorm infection
item.description:
XWorm delivered via Spanish-language invoice lure on September 8, 2026, using a RAR-disguised-as-LZH dropper feeding a JavaScript loader. Infection does not survive reboot, complicating live-system triage.
- Phishing email arrived from amedrano.tornillo@gmail[.]com, relayed through 217.60.195[.]100, with subject "ENVIO DOCUMENTOS FACTURA 4558". The attachment (SHA-256: 9b4e654a8435d91c7f4e24e7fd844cbbb62328131b0065bc5a534c6e948c02c5) presents as an LZH archive but is actually RAR v5, a classic extension-spoofing trick (T1036.008) to confuse users and some security tools.
- Extracted payload is a heavily obfuscated JavaScript file (SHA-256: 5ba1eee1204710adfe1963b730de79c7a8089b173e811052e7be464fc5da1a1d, 207 KB) named to match the lure. JS-based loaders drop directly into script host processes like wscript.exe or cscript.exe; look for those spawning unusual child processes or making outbound TCP connections.
- XWorm C2 communicated over raw TCP to 43.228.157[.]141:7007, a non-HTTP channel that bypasses many proxy-based controls. Pivot on port 7007 outbound in your network logs and flag any wscript or cscript process with external TCP connections.
- The infection did not persist across reboot, meaning volatile memory and live network state are your primary evidence sources. Capture RAM and full PCAP before pulling the plug; post-reboot, most artifacts may be gone.
PCAP, malware samples, and notes are available in the MTA zip packages.

item.title: Panzer ransomware targets Italian manufacturer as ESXi capability raises industrial security concerns
item.description:

- Panzer launched in August 2026 as a semi-open RaaS, recruiting affiliates via Tox with an 80/20 revenue split. Builds support Windows, Linux, VMware ESXi, and FreeBSD with 15+ customizable commands and anti-detection features. No verified samples or network IOCs have been released, making behavior-based detection the only current option.
- The ESXi capability is the critical technical detail. A single hypervisor compromise can encrypt dozens of VMs simultaneously, extending recovery timelines far beyond endpoint-only incidents. Italian 🇮🇹 victims Doimo Cucine (30 GB claimed) and NTE Italia (16 GB claimed) were posted four days apart, matching Panzer's top sectors: technology (25%) and manufacturing (19%).
- Estimated dwell time is 5-12 days from access to encryption, with exfiltration starting within 48-72 hours of domain-level access. TTPs attributed with medium-to-low confidence include credential dumping, brute force, network discovery, lateral movement via remote services and valid accounts, and security tool impairment.
Hunt for anomalous large outbound transfers to non-corporate cloud storage in that 48-72 hour post-domain-compromise window. Isolate ESXi management interfaces and backup systems from general networks.

item.title: Unmasking SCCM Application Execution
item.description:
SCCM application execution hides behind WmiPrvSE.exe, not CcmExec.exe, making it far harder to detect than script-based SCCM abuse. SpecterOps maps the full DLL chain and delivers a Splunk-based detection strategy.
- Script execution via SCCM (SCCMHunter) produces CcmExec.exe spawning PowerShell.exe directly, easy to catch. Application execution (SharpSCCM exec) goes CcmExec.exe to WmiPrvSE.exe to the payload, because CcmExec.exe loads CITaskMgr.dll, posts task properties to the root\CCM\CIModels WMI namespace via IWbemServices::ExecMethodAsync, and a pre-running WmiPrvSE.exe picks up that task asynchronously.

item.description:

item.title: How to correlate Kubernetes audit logs with container runtime data
item.description:
Kubernetes audit logs and container runtime data answer different questions. Joining them by hand is the only way to see a full container escape, including the tools the runtime never records.
Key findings:
- The two join keys that cover most cases: kubernetes.audit.user.extra.authentication.kubernetes.io/pod-name paired with orchestrator.resource.name when the pod-name extra is present, and kubernetes.audit.objectRef.name plus orchestrator.namespace when the call is attributed only as a service account in user.name. Neither source is complete alone.
- In the EKS lab, a compromised workload service account ran discovery, read secrets, minted a token, created a privileged pod with hostPID, hostIPC, a privileged security context, and a hostPath mount to /, then execed in. The requestObject.spec fields in the audit log exposed that sensitivity; D4C alone would not have shown the pod spec.
- nsenter and chroot never appeared in D4C process events. The runtime recorded only the target process (true in the lab; a shell in a real breakout). The decoded kubernetes.audit.requestURI on the pods/exec event is where the wrapper commands live. If you are only watching runtime, you miss the breakout mechanism entirely.
- user_agent.original on the audit event flagged the SA using python-requests and curl, not a normal in-cluster controller. event.outcome separated forbidden recon from allowed secret reads.

item.title: Linux Detection Engineering - Fileless Execution
item.description:
Linux fileless execution is not invisible: Elastic maps five memfd-based tradecraft patterns to concrete eBPF telemetry starting in Elastic Security 9.4.0, with detection rules and the open-source FENIX lab framework.
- memfd_create is the pivot point. The syscall creates an anonymous memory-backed fd with no path on disk, then the payload is written in and executed via /proc/self/fd/N. Elastic Defend 9.4.0 on kernel 5.10.16+ now records this as a process event with process.Ext.memfd.name and process.Ext.memfd.flags fields, making the full chain queryable: download, memfd_create, exec sequence visible in EQL without relying on procfs paths in child processes. Real-world examples include the malicious sympy-dev PyPI package and VoidLink paired with a rootkit that scanned for memfd-backed PIDs to hide.
- Five distinct execution classes each leave different artifacts: anonymous memfd-backed ELF exec (/proc/self/fd/N as execve path), interpreter one-liners where python3/perl/php calls memfd_create internally, fileless staging via curl/wget piped to an interpreter, deleted-file execution where /proc/PID/exe shows "path (deleted)" while the process runs on an open inode, and fileless LKM loading via finit_module on a memfd fd. Each class needs separate detection logic.
- LKM loading gets new visibility: init_module and finit_module calls now surface as load_module event actions on process events in 9.4.0.

item.title: Improper OTP Implementation to Full Account Takeover
item.description:

item.title: Token Analysis and Tracking System (TATS)
item.description:

It visualizes exchanges as Mermaid graphs and sequence diagrams, tracks refresh token chains, and flags FOCI and brokered client ID (BroCI) behavior specific to Microsoft's OAuth deviations.
- Audience mismatch: tokens issued with management.core.windows[.]net as the aud claim were accepted by management.azure[.]com and portal.azure[.]com, meaning Microsoft is not strictly enforcing audience binding as OAuth spec requires.
- Pre-MFA token issuance: after username and password entry, access and refresh tokens were issued before the MFA prompt appeared. The amr claim confirmed MFA was absent. While the portal itself enforced MFA, those tokens could be brokered to nested apps like Key Vault if no explicit Conditional Access Policy (CAP) covered them.
- The CAP gap is the real risk: relying solely on MFA enforcement at the admin portal level leaves nested applications exposed to token brokering abuse if they lack their own CAP.
Defenders: audit your CAPs to confirm MFA is required at the resource level, not just the portal.

item.title: Dissecting a PHP web server rootkit
item.description:
A fileless PHP web shell implant targeting F5 BIG-IP APM systems uses custom ELF loading, APR function hooking, and in-memory mmap patching to deliver attacker access with zero on-disk web shell artifacts.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-53521 is the initial access vector: an unauthenticated RCE in BIG-IP APM when an access policy is configured on a virtual server. The second-stage payload (SHA256: 26bd5b0722d1dbab5db749a063c49bc8638653ac2addfead7a9cb3d6d57bccc9, detected as Linux/Agnt-IC) is deployed by a first-stage installer that infects /usr/sbin/httpd and survives BIG-IP upgrade images by targeting /mnt/tm_install workflows.
- Execution begins before Apache's main() by hijacking __libc_start_main via a custom ELF loader that reads /proc/self/exe, manually maps an embedded ELF, and installs a wrapper, giving the implant full API resolution before any application thread starts. RC4 with key TrswBWIl90Z5e38n hides all operational strings at rest.
- The web shell never touches disk. The implant hooks apr_dso_load to detect libphp loading, then patches open, mmap, and fxstat inside libphp to intercept PHP's file reads of apm_css.php3, full_wt.php3, and webtop_popup_css.php3. At mmap time it prepends the embedded PHP payload in memory only. The shell checks for magic prefix BSOHAzPB, decrypts with key wSLjN1beuR, evals, and returns HTTP 201 with Content-Type: text/css to blend in.

item.title: Digital Forensics: Fixing a Corrupted Disk After File Exfiltration
item.description:
Corrupted MBR used to obstruct investigation into insider data exfiltration. NTFS artifacts including $MFT and $UsnJrnl expose the full attack chain despite deliberate anti-forensic wiping.
Key findings:
- The MBR's final two bytes (boot signature 0x55 0xAA) were overwritten to prevent tools like Autopsy and FTK Imager from reading the image. Repair requires a hex editor such as HxD: overwrite, never delete, those bytes to restore the signature before any further analysis.
- After repair, export and parse MFT with MFTECmd.exe (Eric Zimmerman's EZTools): MFTECmd.exe -f ..\Evidence$MFT --csv ..\Evidence\ --csvf MFT.csv. Even deleted file records survive here, revealing Excel sheets, PDFs, and zip archives flagged as sensitive corporate data.
- $UsnJrnl (J) logged the full exfiltration sequence: a folder named "data Exfil" was created, files were appended to "New Compressed (zipped) Folder.zip", then renamed and deleted. Parse J with MFTECmd, open in Timeline Explorer, and filter Update Reason to FileDelete.
- DiskWipe.exe was found on the second partition. To confirm execution and tie actions to a user, extend the investigation into Prefetch, Shellbags, registry, and NTUSER.DAT.
Always hash-verify the forensic image before touching it, then work only on a verified copy. MFT and $UsnJrnl together reconstruct what wipers try to erase.
